The threat to California's bridges has officials up and down the West Coast asking "what if?" Portland, Oregon is the nation's 26th largest city and has 10 bridges over the Willamette River. Mayor Vera Katz drove across one of them during rush hour to join us tonight. Mayor, welcome, and how was the security tonight on the bridge compared to usual nights?
Good evening. The security was tight. We are on very high alert here.
Now when you say the security is tight, what do you mean?

Well, we have the waterways and the airspace covered. We have our traffic division and our specialty units around the bridgeheads, under the bridges, along the waterfront. We're working in cooperation with southwest and Washington, with the sheriff's office, with the coast guard, with our own fire bureau ships. So we have really focused our attention at the bridges.

Here's what I don't understand, Mayor, and maybe you can help me out a little bit, is that in most cities, I think in probably cities that cars aren't being stopped before they go over the bridge. Give me a hint, though. Give me a hint though. How are you going to prevent -- if I were in a car and it was -- and I had it full of explosives and I headed for your bridge, how are you going to prevent that?

Well, there are situations -- if the car is rolling on the bridge and you have no clue whatsoever, then you have a dangerous situation. If there are objects on the bridge or suspicious individuals taking photographs of the bridges, we're there immediately to put a halt to that activity.

I want to talk about the revelation that the strain that killed this woman in New York is called indistinguishable from the one that was on Senator Daschle's letter. Does that mean they're the same?

That's right, Greta, and that's an important point to make because so far, all the anthrax that's been recovered has been the same strain. It either is or is closely related to one called the Ames Strain. So clearly, this is all the same source material. You couldn't conceive that two different groups would be mailing out the same strain of bacteria here.
John, does that mean though -- is there a huge amount of Ames Strain so that it really doesn't help us much in the investigation and lots of people could have it?

Well, lots of people could have it, but it helps us because it identifies or narrows the field down to a small group of individuals who could be doing this. When you put it together with the other evidence that's available, for instance, all the letters were sent by the same -- all the letters that have been recovered were sent by the same individual or the same group. The strain is the same. None of it is resistant to antibiotics. Clearly, this is a single point source and that's an important piece of information.

John, we're clamping down now, or at least I assume everyone is, on the anthrax bacteria, to make sure that bad things don't happen. But prior to September 11, how easily could I get a hold of the Ames Strain?

Well, not very easily within the last year because the CDC has a select agent list and bacillus anthraces, the bacterium that we -- that is used to make the anthrax is on that list. So there were 66 laboratories in the United States that registered and before they could transfer that to another laboratory or to another individual, that individual would also have to be registered. Now, merely the possession of it is required as a registration required. And so it would have been very difficult anytime within the last year. Before that, it might have been a little bit easier but you really don't have to get from someone who has it. Remember, these anthrax spores exist in the environment. So it's possible for someone to have gone to an area and actually grown this up themselves.

As you listen to all the reports, John, and the FBI briefings and the attorney general -- when you listen to them, what question do you have for the investigators? What do you think is sort of the key clue you're looking for?

Well, I guess from a microbiological point-of-view, the real question for me is why you have two different grades of material. What that clearly points to is someone who's making this material and not someone who has purchased this material from, say, a third country. And the reason for that is that to have the crude material almost suggests a processing step, that is, you make the crude material, and that is on the way to making purified material. The September 18 letters that went out had a cruder preparation in them. It looks like they waited to see what effect they were going to get. October the 5th, we have a death. October the 6th, we're all aware of it. On October the 9th, the second letter or group of letters went out with a more highly purified material from the same batch of crew material that went out on the 18th. Well, the refinement issue is the question because we've been hearing a lot about whether or not they added an additive to this, something called bentonite. It's actually -- there are a group of additives that you could add to it. What we don't know is what the length of processing time is. My suspicion is, I know that to make the bacteria is an overnight process. To make the spores is an overnight process. So you're really not talking about but a week or two in order to amass an amount of material. What we don't know is how much they have and how much that processed for that final step and that's going to require some investigation to find that out.

John, the FBI director made a call for help if anyone had seen anything unusual. What would I be looking for in terms of the unusual? What is it -- something, as a layperson, that might give me a clue if someone is involved in this?

Well, if someone has been growing up a large amount of the material, there's going to be byproduct and the byproduct might not look like the normal things that you would see in someone's trash. If someone is using a ferment or a large capacity vessel for liquid cultures, they're going to have to have a way to sterilize that medium to go in there and then they're going to have to weigh -- have a way of disposing of that after the fact. So if someone is seeing some foul smelling liquid laying around or has noticed that there's something out of place that doesn't look it's normal trash processing in a neighborhood environment that might tell you. It also requires some fairly sophisticated laboratory equipment. I think that's why, right now, the FBI is looking at those 66 laboratories that have reported that they have anthrax because it almost seems like you have to have a very technologically, sophisticated laboratory to get this to this stage.

text: It was last June as a matter of fact, when I was trying to get to Osama Bin Laden and had three confirmations from different sources that I was expected in Kandahar between June 1 and June 4. Yes, but I also got the feeling that he wanted to somehow dissolve or resolve the Osama Bin Laden problem. I got the feeling that Osama was an albatross around his neck, was responsible for all the sanctions that had been imposed in Afghanistan. And I also get the feeling, reconstructing a lot of what has happened before and since, that we were very inflexible in our demands. We said, in all the private negotiations that were going on at the time that we wanted Osama Bin Laden delivered to us on a silver platter. There was no flexibility. They did want to explore alternative compromises. We say now that they were stalling. On the other hand, we never bothered to explore anything beyond given to us with no questions -- no further questions asked.
And what kind of -- though Arnaud, what kind of alternative or flexible conditions could there be with the father-in- the-law of Osama Bin Laden, the supreme leader of the Taliban?

Well, one was suggested by President Musharraf himself when I interviewed him last March. And that was to have a tribunal of distinguished Islamic scholars. One from Saudi Arabia. One from Afghanistan. And one from the neutral Muslim country, that would be chosen by the United States. And they would then examine the evidence that we had against Osama bin Laden. But all these things were never explored. We just said, "Hand him over," and that's all.

In fact, that was the lead to my story when I came out of Afghanistan. Any fatwa issued by Osama bin Laden, declaring war on the United States and ordering Muslims to kill Americans was null and void because Osama bin Laden had absolutely no religious, legal right to issue such a fatwa, given the fact that he had not completed 12 years of religious education. Only seven years as Mullah Omar himself has only done seven years of religious education. And as was pointed out at the beginning of this program, is called a mullah, but is not really a mullah. So...

I thought that it was tense. I know today the conventional wisdom that it's very, very close. It was tense. On the other hand, he could not put any daylight between himself and Osama bin Laden, given the fact that there are 40 some, 30 to 40,000 Afghan Arabs, who are acting as Praetorian Guard to Osama bin Laden and are far more powerful than any forces that can be deployed by Mullah Omar.
Before I let you go, what were the living conditions that he was living in when you met him?
My pleasure, thank you.

text: Yes, they are.
Why?

Why? Because we've been hearing stories, not just her story, but many workers that work at the site, many residents have been complaining, similar to her complaints. But most of all, we've been hearing reports in places like Mt. Sinai Clinic, that have analyzed and diagnosed many workers and residents with occupational asthma and other serious respiratory problems.
Bill, have you checked the air in the region to see whether or not there's anything in there that can be hazardous to people's health?

That's what we have been doing, Greta, from day one. We've set up an elaborate monitoring stations, over 19 right now that are operational. And we're providing information to people to make judgments for themselves. But also, we're interpreting that information from ground zero.
Let me ask you. When you say monitoring stations, how far are the monitoring stations from the World Trade Center site?

We have monitoring stations right at the World Trade Center. And we have monitoring stations that go back away from the site. Our building is, for instance, only six to eight blocks away from that site. And we are monitoring station on our building.
What are you looking for?
We're looking for asbestos and air. We're looking for PCBs. We've looked for benzenes, volatile organic compounds, dioxins. We're looking for a variety of chemicals that cause concern to people.
Joel, what's wrong with the monitoring done by the EPA, if anything?

In some ways -- well, it could be better. I don't think they're looking extensively for all the ingredients. And also, they could spread their monitors out. Some of the things that were spotted near the site, when people complain, they said this has been monitored outside the site. We're calling for more extensive monitoring. But what's really important here is that the information that they found that they gave to us after somewhat of a little bit of a fight, after we filed a FOIA request, this was never published on their web site in the first two weeks of the -- after the World Trade Center disaster. And that's the information that was really needed by the firefighters and the rescue workers.
All right, well, now that -- let me ask you, the information they did finally put on the web site or disclose, did that meet the EPA minimum standards?

I mean, it exceeded some of the minimum standards. And this is out of their quotes. On September 23rd, EPA identified elevated levels of benzene. Dioxin, 10 samples were collected on October 2 and analyzed for dioxin and fuorons. Four of these samples showed results above the guideline level, in which EPA would take some type of action and reduce people's exposure.

Joel, let me -- I guess I can hear what he's saying in terms of what the EPA has, you know, failed to put on their web site according to you. But you know, this problem wasn't started by the EPA. What do you expect them to do? I mean, they didn't fly these planes and create this hazardous scene.

I'm not accusing them of doing that. What I'm saying is that it's partly their job, along with the New York City Department of Health and DEP to inform people of the reports and the information that they got, that they worked on, that told us that things were safe. And yet, their own data shows that it's not safe. And I think what happened is it's not just the environmental community. It's doctors and medical institutions need this data to advise people what to look for and what to be aware of. And what turns out that this data shows that there's many, many problems that exceeded levels of concern. And part of the problem is that many landlords and employers are telling their employees and the residents to go back because it is safe. And we did find asbestos levels above 1 percent, 2 percent, 3 percent, even 5 percent, which requires proper asbestos abatement. And yet, we've heard case after case of landlords and employers telling the workers to go back to work.
Ritu, to you, are you satisfied or dissatisfied with the information that you've received and the monitoring by the EPA?

Well, I'm dissatisfied just because we clear conflicting things. And I feel like there's one authority on anything. The EPA says, you know, the EPA and city officials and government officials are saying it's OK. Other private agencies, who do testing. say the levels are much higher. So no, I'm not really satisfied. And it kind of leaves us up in arms because we don't know who to look for, for the right advice and who is -- you know, we all care to get New York back up on its feet. And as a New Yorker, I strongly want to get back to some normalcy, but not at the risk of my health. and my neighbors feel the same way.
All right, we're going to take a quick break. When we come back, we'll talk to Bill Muszynski to see if there's anything the EPA can do to satisfy many of the New Yorkers.

Tonight's "Flashpoint" is anger at ground zero. You're looking at a live picture of ground zero. Is living by or working at the World Trade Center disaster site hazardous to everyone's health? On my POINT panel are EPA acting regional administrator Bill Muszynski, Ritu Upadhyay, who lives near the disaster scene, and environmental attorney, Joel Kupferman. Bill, to you. What can the EPA do? Is it EPA's job merely to monitor the level of the contaminants in the air or can you actually do something?

We are doing something. And I think what you just heard said is why people, why citizens are upset. The data that Joel mentioned are at site. The benzene level at the immediate site at the toe where the material comes out of the air. And we have explained, and our web site clearly explains the difference between taking a high reading at the site and a reading off of the site, where people and workers are.

But that makes me wonder then, Bill. I realize that the levels may be high at the work site, but suppose I live up ten blocks. And three years from now, I have a very low level because the wind has carried it up there. Am I at risk?

That's where our monitors are set up also to define. We set standards based upon a 30 year risk. And then we have backed them up so that we look at what is a one-year risk at this site, since it's expected that this will not go beyond that period of time to provide assurances that is there is no significant risk to people. The 1 percent asbestos in dust, we've told people when you go in your apartment and you have dust in it, you should assume there's a hazard there. That should be cleaned professionally and monitored after it's cleaned. So I don't -- I think the misinformation that people are getting through reports like were in "The Daily News" the other week are causing concerns. And we are concerned about the people. We report the data.
Joel, do you agree with him?

Well, to say there's no monitoring reports. On September 19th and 20, which included samples from the general area of Stuyvesant High School, which is above the site and Battery Park, 12 of the 24 samples showed asbestos levels slightly above the EPA levels of concern. But all this information wasn't published to the public. I mean, it took us a while to get it out there.

So Joel, is your complaint not with the EPA, not with the way they're doing the monitoring, not with what they're doing, but for what you may think is perhaps being asleep at the wheel getting information out? Is that the complaint?
Well, also I think that there could have been better monitoring from the beginning, but also really concerned about the work.
Well, give me an idea. What -- I mean -- first of all, if it's safe, the monitoring isn't so much an issue. It's whether or not there's a problem that we need to watch out with. But...

OK, as you see, the people on the screen now, they're not wearing masks. All right, law, OSHA law and federal regulations, these people should be wearing masks. Not the light paper mask you just saw now. What's interesting is the information took a while to get out, but someone from the NIEH, the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences went down to the site, and studied there for a while. And he said the injury and illness reports for the initial weeks of the search and rescue activity were unacceptable levels. Moreover, the exposure data, as well as the potential for serious exposure to toxic materials, including asbestos among the construction response workers raises significant concerns. Accordingly, how do respond to such issues demands serious attention in the context of worker protection and training needs.
Joel, is that a problem though with the EPA? Or is it a problem with the firefighters or perhaps their union and their organization for not supplying them with the proper equipment?
I'd say it's partly both, because when I spoke with construction workers and safety workers, what I asked them, "Where is our masks?" And they told me that EPA administrator said it was safe.

That's not true. That is not true and you know it. The EPA administrator went there on Thursday night, right after the site. She walked that site. She held up the proper equipment. We have provided hundreds of thousands of dollars of equipment. And that's exactly what I'm saying. I think that is an incorrect statement, Joel. And you have no basis to say that.
If you check news releases, which I don't have here.

Baloney. She was at the site in front of TV cameras. The workers at that site we have said consistently should be wearing the protective equipment that we have provided through the city and the state.
Ritu, are you ever going to feel comfortable going back to your apartment?

I don't think I will honestly, Greta, in the next six months. Maybe a year from now, I'd be OK living there. But you know, buildings are going to continue to be demolished, according to some reports over the next six months. And I could move back in next week. And a building could, you know, be demolished, you know, a block down from me. And then, I don't know. Will it release more toxins into the air, who knows? There's too much uncertainty right now. And this debate in and of itself is alarming. Because who has the answers?
What answers -- what are the specific questions you would like answered, Ritu, that would make you feel safer or at least have more information?

You know, I'd at least like to know what is going to happen five years from now. I mean, they say OK, there's no significant risk. If you are healthy right now, you'll be OK. But what does that mean, you know, for someone like me who has a mother and three siblings -- and her three siblings who've had cancer? For my neighbor who has asthma, who can't stay there for longer than 20 minutes. What's going to happen five years from now? Can anyone say with any assurance there's not going to be any long-term chronic health effects, any diseases? And it's not just asbestos. It's not just the benzene. It's not just the PCBs, but the cumulative effect of all of these. Have there really been any substantial studies done? You know, I know there's a lot of occupational studies that have been done of workers who have exposed to certain levels of any one of these. But what's the cumulative effect of all of these? I just think that I'm not comfortable with the information and the studies that are out there.

And hopefully, as time goes on, we'll get more information. And hopefully, it is not dangerous. My thanks tonight to Bill Muszynski, Ritu Upadhyay, and Joel Kupferman. THE POINT will be right back after a quick break and our "MONEYLINE Update."

December 9 is when they were retreating from the Tora Bora area across the border into Pakistan. I was in the area two days later, on December 11, which had just been occupied by Pakistani troops which have been kept out of there since their independence. You'd have riots all over Pakistan.

When Osama came across, apparently there were only 50 people with him, and they then got into smaller vehicles to drive into Peshawar. As for the next terrorist targets, nobody really knows. And I think a lot of this information has been put out by al Qaeda and its operatives to destabilize the United States, to demoralize the United States. My guess is that the next major terrorist movement will take place in the Persian Gulf, either in a Saudi oil terminal, a Saudi -- the nerve center of Saudi oil fields, which is called Abcaque (ph) -- or perhaps sinking a super tanker in the straights of Hormuz, which is very easily done at night from a rubber boat, sticking a bunch of limpid mines on the waterline of a super tanker. Nobody believes in the $25 million reward that I've talked to.

They don't believe that it's for real. So I don't think that's going to work in terms of bringing somebody forward. I think he has control of the security forces. I don't think he has total control of the famous or infamous ISI, Inter- Services Intelligence agency.

I don't know about protecting him, because I think that in Peshawar, a city of 3.5 million, he has zillions of supporters and people willing to hide him. But that ISI has a rough idea of where he is, I have no doubt.
Mr. De Borchgrave, thank you very much for dropping by in person. Appreciate your time.
